policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All residents, representatives, family members and visitors who raise a concern; the Manager, Alternate Manager and all staff who receive complaints
policies.purpose: To give residents an established, prompt and retaliation-free way to raise complaints, and to use the results to correct problems and improve care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows residents to make complaints without threat or fear of retaliation, and responds promptly through an established procedure, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(q)–(r). Residents are informed of, and may use, the complaint procedures of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, local Adult Protective Services, the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) and the designated protection and advocacy agency (COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(s)). This written complaint and grievance policy is one of the policies OHCQ reviews at survey. Every grievance is logged, assigned to a named person, answered within the time set below, and tracked to an outcome. Any complaint that alleges abuse, neglect or financial exploitation is handled under SAF-01 and reported within 24 hours.

definitions.definition: Any concern or expression of dissatisfaction about care, services, staff, other residents, the environment or the facility's practices, whether made verbally or in writing.
A complaint that is logged and tracked through this procedure to resolution and response.
Any threat, discharge, transfer, reduction in services or change in treatment because a person made a complaint.
A written plan submitted to OHCQ describing how the facility will correct a cited deficiency.

procedures: The Manager designates a Grievance Coordinator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless otherwise assigned in writing) and posts the Coordinator's name and how to reach them next to the posted Bill of Rights.

Residents may submit a complaint verbally, in writing, through a representative, or anonymously. A suggestion box with blank grievance forms is kept in a common area, and staff will complete a form for any resident who asks.
Any staff member who receives a complaint writes it down the same shift, using the grievance form, and gives it to the Grievance Coordinator by the end of that shift.
If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation or an injury of unknown origin, the staff member notifies the Manager immediately and the report is made under SAF-01 within 24 hours.
The Coordinator enters the grievance in the grievance log on the day received, recording the date, the complainant, the nature of the concern and the staff assigned.
The Coordinator acknowledges the complaint to the resident in person or in writing within one business day, using the resident's preferred language or communication method (RR-08).
The Coordinator investigates by interviewing the resident and staff involved, reviewing records and observing the issue. Investigators must not be the person the complaint is against.

The Coordinator takes immediate action to protect the resident when there is a safety risk, and takes steps to prevent retaliation, including a check-in with the resident within 7 days after resolution.

The Manager gives the resident or representative a written or verbal response stating what was found and what will be done, within 5 business days of receipt. If more time is needed, the Coordinator tells the resident why and gives a firm date.
The Coordinator asks the resident whether they are satisfied. If not, the matter goes to the Administrator for review, who responds in writing within 7 days.

At every step, the resident is told that they may contact the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, local Adult Protective Services, OHCQ at (410) 402-8217 or (800) 492-6005, or the protection and advocacy agency, at any time, and that using the internal process is not required first (RR-03).

Staff must not discourage a resident from complaining, must not interfere with calls or letters to outside agencies, and must not retaliate. Staff who retaliate are subject to discipline up to termination (STF-06).

The Coordinator records the outcome, corrective action and date closed in the log, and files the grievance form in a grievance file, with a copy of any resident-specific outcome placed in the resident record if it affects care (REC-01).
The Coordinator reviews the log monthly for trends, and the Administrator presents the results at each quality assurance meeting (GOV-04).
When OHCQ cites a complaint-related deficiency, the Administrator prepares and submits the plan of correction within the time OHCQ sets and keeps a copy with the survey file (GOV-02).
New staff are trained on this policy at orientation, and all staff are retrained annually (STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews unresolved grievances, ensures prompt response, supplies resources for corrective action and prepares any plan of correction.
Logs, investigates, tracks and answers each grievance and checks for retaliation.
Ensures staff receive and forward complaints, and approves the response to the resident.
Receive complaints respectfully, record them the same shift and never retaliate.
May raise concerns at any time through the internal process or directly with outside agencies.

documentation: Grievance forms
Grievance log with dates, handler, response date and outcome
Written responses to residents
Retaliation check-in notes
Quality assurance meeting minutes
Plans of correction and OHCQ correspondence
Staff training records

policies.title: Ombudsman and Agency Access
policies.applies_to: All residents and representatives; the Manager, Alternate Manager and all staff; Ombudsman, OHCQ, Adult Protective Services and protection and advocacy representatives who visit the facility
policies.purpose: To make sure residents can contact and meet with the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and state agencies, and that required reporting signs and information are posted and current.
policies.policy: Residents have access to the complaint procedures of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, local Adult Protective Services (APS), the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) and the designated protection and advocacy agency, as provided in COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(s). [AGENCY NAME] does not restrict, delay, monitor or discourage contact with these agencies. Abuse, neglect and financial exploitation reporting signs are posted in employee and public areas, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.37G. Reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation are made within 24 hours to law enforcement, OHCQ, the Ombudsman or local area agency on aging, local APS and the Manager (COMAR 10.07.14.37C).

definitions.definition: The state and local advocate program, operated through the Maryland Department of Aging and local area agencies on aging, that receives and resolves complaints on behalf of residents.
The local Department of Social Services unit that investigates abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults.
The state-designated agency that protects the legal rights of people with disabilities.
The Department of Aging's information and referral resource at 844-627-5465.

procedures: The Manager posts, next to the Bill of Rights and in a place residents can read without asking, contact information for the local Ombudsman ([PHONE]), local APS ([PHONE]), OHCQ ((410) 402-8217 / (800) 492-6005), the protection and advocacy agency ([PHONE]) and Maryland Access Point (844-627-5465).

The Manager posts the abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting signs in each employee area (break room or time clock area) and in each public area (entrance and main common room) and confirms by monthly walk-through that signs are present and legible.
At admission, the Manager or designee tells each resident and representative how to reach each agency, gives them a printed contact sheet and records this in the admission checklist.
Residents may use a private phone, mail, email or the facility phone to contact an agency. Staff provide a private space and assist with dialing, writing or large-print materials on request (RR-08).

Staff allow the Ombudsman, OHCQ surveyors, APS and the protection and advocacy agency to enter the facility, talk with residents privately and review the records the law allows them to review. The Manager is notified on arrival, but staff do not delay access while waiting for the Manager.

Staff must not ask a resident why they are meeting with an agency, must not sit in on private interviews unless the resident requests it, and must not retaliate against residents who talk with agencies.
When the Ombudsman or another agency makes a request for records, the Manager releases only what the agency is entitled to under law, following RR-07, and documents what was provided and when.

On any abuse, neglect or exploitation allegation, the staff member who learns of it tells the Manager at once, and the Manager makes the report within 24 hours to law enforcement, OHCQ, the Ombudsman or local area agency on aging, local APS and the Manager as required by COMAR 10.07.14.37C. Details are in SAF-01.
The Manager keeps a copy of every report and confirmation of the date and time it was made. The facility understands that failure to report within 3 days can result in a penalty of up to $1,000.
Within 7 days of receiving a survey report or Ombudsman finding, the Manager reviews it with the Administrator and assigns corrective action (GOV-02).
The Manager reviews and updates agency contact information at least quarterly and whenever an agency notifies the facility of a change, and records the review date on the posting.
Staff receive training on resident access to agencies and on the posted signs at orientation and annually (STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the facility does not restrict agency access and reviews agency findings.
Keeps postings current, gives residents contact information, grants agency access and makes required reports.
Performs these duties when the Manager is absent.
Provide immediate access and help residents contact agencies, and report allegations to the Manager at once.

documentation: Photograph or log of postings and monthly walk-through checks
Admission checklist showing contact sheet provided
Agency visit log (agency, date, purpose)
Copies of abuse, neglect and exploitation reports with confirmation of date and time
Records-release log
Agency findings and corrective action notes
Training records

policies.title: Resident Agreement, Fees, Deposits and Refunds
policies.applies_to: All applicants, residents and representatives; the Administrator, Manager, business office and admissions staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that every resident understands in writing what services and charges apply, that charges change only with proper notice, and that refunds and final accounts are handled on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the OHCQ sample resident agreement template, with the required nonfinancial and financial terms, for every resident. The agreement states the financial terms of the stay, including fees and what they cover. The agreement discloses whether adult medical day care is available and the facility's policies on it, and attendance is voluntary (COMAR 10.07.14.36D(2)). The facility gives at least 45 calendar days' written notice of a rate increase (COMAR 10.07.14.27). A Uniform Disclosure Statement is given to anyone who asks, free of charge, and is included in marketing materials (COMAR 10.07.14.10). Within 30 calendar days after discharge, the facility gives a final statement of account, pays any refund due and returns all money and property (COMAR 10.07.14.34G). For residents on the Community Options Waiver, the facility charges no more than $420 per month for room and board, because the waiver pays for services only (COMAR 10.09.54.03D).

definitions.definition: The written contract between the facility and the resident or representative that states services, rates, charges, house rules and rights.
The OHCQ form describing the services, staffing, fees and policies of the facility.
A written itemization of all charges, payments, credits and refunds owed at the end of a resident's stay.
Charges for housing, meals and related non-service items. For a waiver participant, limited to $420 per month.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the resident agreement on the current OHCQ sample template, with all required nonfinancial and financial terms completed for this facility's level of care and services, and reviews it annually and whenever the regulation or template changes (GOV-03).

Before admission, the Manager or admissions staff gives the applicant and representative the draft agreement, the Uniform Disclosure Statement, the Bill of Rights and the house rules, and allows time to read them and consult an advisor or attorney before signing.

The staff member reviews the agreement line by line, including fees, what each fee covers, extra charges for added services, adult medical day care availability and policies, notice terms, and the resident's right to terminate (ADM-07), and uses the resident's preferred language (RR-08).

The resident or representative signs and dates the agreement along with an authorized facility representative. A copy is given to the resident or representative the same day, and the original is placed in the resident record (REC-01).

The facility collects a pre-admission deposit only if permitted by COMAR 10.07.14 and only on terms written in the agreement. The agreement states the amount, what it is for, and how and when any unused amount is returned. Staff give a written receipt for every payment.

For a waiver participant, the facility bills Medicaid only for services covered by the waiver and charges the resident no more than $420 per month for room and board. The business office checks each waiver resident's invoice before it is issued (GOV-06).

The facility never charges a waiver participant for a covered service, never asks for payment beyond the room and board limit, and never requires private-pay supplements as a condition of admission or retention.

The Administrator gives each resident and representative at least 45 calendar days' written notice before any rate increase takes effect. The notice states the old rate, the new rate, the effective date and the reason, and a copy is filed in the resident record.

When service needs change under the service plan (ADM-04) and a charge changes, the Manager reviews and updates the agreement with the resident or representative in writing before the new charge starts.
When the facility changes any service, the Administrator files an amended Uniform Disclosure Statement with OHCQ within 30 days of the change and keeps the filing confirmation (GOV-02).

The Uniform Disclosure Statement is given free to anyone who asks, and the current version is included in the facility's marketing materials. Staff check marketing items quarterly to confirm they include the current version.

When a resident is discharged, transferred or dies, the business office prepares a final statement of account that lists all charges, payments, credits and the refund due, and the Administrator reviews and signs it.

Within 30 calendar days of the discharge date, the business office sends the final statement, pays any refund due to the resident or the resident's estate, and returns all money and property, and the Manager documents the date and method used (RR-05, ADM-06).
Residents and representatives may dispute any charge through the grievance process (RR-02), and the Administrator responds in writing.
The Administrator reviews agreement, rate notice and refund files each quarter, and reports findings in the quality assurance review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the agreement template, approves rates, issues rate notices, files amended disclosure statements and signs final statements.
Reviews the agreement with residents, obtains signatures and keeps the agreement current with service plan changes.
Issue invoices, apply the $420 room and board limit for waiver residents, and prepare refunds and final statements on time.
Read the agreement, pay agreed charges and raise questions or disputes.

Signed receipt for the Uniform Disclosure Statement
Deposit receipts
Rate increase notices with delivery proof

Waiver resident invoices showing room and board charge

Quarterly file review notes

policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: All residents and representatives; the Administrator, Manager, business office staff and any staff who handle resident money or property
policies.purpose: To protect residents' money and belongings from loss, misuse or exploitation, and to ensure that any funds the facility handles are held lawfully, separately and with full records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may decline to handle resident funds. If the facility handles a resident's funds, it does so only on the express written request of the resident or the resident's agent (COMAR 10.07.14.39B–C). Resident funds of $300 or more are deposited in an interest-bearing account, interest belongs to the resident, and resident accounts are kept separate from facility accounts. The facility carries a bond, letter of credit or net assets equal to the average monthly balance of resident funds, with the State as obligee, and keeps the instrument or asset list on site for OHCQ (COMAR 10.07.14.39E). Residents keep their personal clothing and effects with reasonable security (COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(n)). Funds and property are returned within 30 calendar days of discharge (COMAR 10.07.14.34G). Misuse of resident funds is exploitation and is reported under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: Money belonging to a resident that the facility holds or manages on the resident's behalf.
A signed, dated written instruction from the resident or the resident's agent asking the facility to manage funds.
A person authorized by the resident, for example through a power of attorney, to act for the resident on financial matters.
The average total of all resident funds held by the facility over a month, which sets the minimum amount of bond, letter of credit or net assets required.
Clothing, furniture, jewelry, devices and other possessions that belong to the resident.

procedures: The Administrator decides, and records in writing, whether the facility will handle resident funds. If the facility will not, the resident agreement says so and staff refer residents to their representative, bank or family for money management.

If the facility handles funds, staff accept them only after the resident or agent signs and dates a written request that names the funds to be held, the purpose and who may authorize withdrawals. Staff verify the agent's authority by reviewing the power of attorney or other authority and file a copy.

Staff must never require a resident to hand over funds as a condition of admission or services, and must not use resident funds to pay facility charges unless the resident or agent authorizes it in writing.

The business office deposits any resident's funds of $300 or more in an interest-bearing account. Interest is credited to the resident. Resident funds are kept in accounts separate from facility operating accounts and are never commingled.

The business office keeps an individual transaction record for each resident that shows the date, type of transaction, amount, the staff member who made it, and the running balance. Each deposit and withdrawal is supported by a signed receipt.

Two staff members, or one staff member and the resident, count and sign for any cash received or paid out. Withdrawals are made only with the resident's or agent's authorization, and the resident signs for any cash received.

The Administrator obtains and keeps on site a bond, letter of credit or net assets equal to the average monthly balance of resident funds, with the State as obligee, and recalculates the required amount each month. The instrument or asset list is available to OHCQ on request.

The business office gives each resident or representative a statement of account on request, within 5 business days, and the Manager offers a statement at least quarterly to each resident whose funds are held.

The Administrator reconciles each account monthly. A second person who does not handle the funds reviews the reconciliation, and both sign and date it. Any discrepancy is reported to the Administrator at once and investigated.
Suspected theft, misuse or exploitation of a resident's money is reported under SAF-01 within 24 hours. The Attorney General may investigate abuse of funds.

On admission, staff inventory the resident's belongings with the resident or representative, record the items in the record, and give the resident a copy. Staff update the inventory when items are added or removed.

Residents may keep their personal clothing and effects. The facility provides a lockable drawer or other reasonable means of security, and staff do not take or restrict personal property except as the resident agrees or as law requires. Valuables the resident asks the facility to hold are stored in a locked area and receipted.

If a resident's property is reported missing, staff take the report the same day, search, notify the Manager and the resident or representative, and record the outcome. The Manager follows the grievance process (RR-02) and reports suspected theft.

When the facility changes ownership, the prior owner gives the new owner a certified audit of resident funds and receipts for all funds, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.39J, and the new owner keeps them on file.

At discharge, transfer or death, the business office completes the final accounting and returns all funds and property, with an inventory signed by the recipient, within 30 calendar days of discharge (RR-04, ADM-06, HCS-09).
Every year the Administrator reviews resident funds practices, bond coverage and account reconciliations, and includes results in the quality assurance review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether to handle funds, maintains the bond or net asset coverage, reviews reconciliations and ensures timely returns of funds and property.
Keep separate accounts and transaction records, issue receipts and statements, and reconcile monthly.
Oversees personal property inventories, security measures and lost property reports.
Never take or borrow resident money or property and report suspected misuse at once.
Give or withdraw written authorization and review statements.

Copy of power of attorney or agent authority
Individual resident transaction records and receipts

Statements given to residents
Personal property inventories

policies.title: Advance Directives and MOLST
policies.applies_to: All residents and representatives; the Manager, delegating nurse, medication technicians, direct care staff and any staff who respond to a medical emergency or arrange a transfer
policies.purpose: To make sure residents' wishes about treatment are asked about, recorded, available when needed and honored, without the facility giving legal advice or making treatment decisions for residents.
policies.policy: The resident record includes any advance directive, mental health advance directive and Maryland Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (MOLST) form (COMAR 10.07.14.29A(7)–(8)). Advance directives, the MOLST form, powers of attorney and guardianship orders are attached to the emergency data sheet that goes with a resident to an acute care facility (COMAR 10.07.14.34F(9)). Residents may make an informed decision to accept or refuse treatment (COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(f)). Staff do not give legal advice and refer residents to counsel (COMAR 10.07.14.36A(1)(l)). The facility does not require a resident to have or not have an advance directive as a condition of admission or care.

definitions.definition: A written statement of a person's wishes about future health care, or the appointment of someone to make health care decisions if the person cannot.
A written statement of a person's preferences for mental health treatment or the appointment of an agent to make mental health decisions.
The Maryland Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment form, a medical order completed by a practitioner that states a resident's treatment preferences, including resuscitation.
The summary of identification, health and contact information and documents that accompanies a resident who is transferred to an acute care facility.
A court order appointing a person to make decisions for a resident.

procedures: During pre-admission screening, the Manager or delegating nurse asks each applicant and representative whether the applicant has an advance directive, a mental health advance directive, a MOLST form, a power of attorney or a guardianship order, and records the answers on the admission checklist.

If the resident has any of these documents, the staff member gets a copy and places it in the designated section of the resident record (REC-01) where all staff can find it at once, including in an emergency, and writes the date received.

If a resident does not have an advance directive or MOLST form, the Manager may offer written information and suggest the resident talk with their practitioner, a family member or an attorney. The facility does not pressure the resident to complete any document.

Staff do not give legal advice, do not interpret a document in a legal sense, and do not witness or help draft a legal document for a resident. If a resident asks about legal matters, staff refer the resident to an attorney or the Ombudsman, and note that referral was made.

A MOLST form must be completed and signed by the resident's practitioner as the law requires. Staff may help a resident make an appointment with the practitioner but do not complete the form on the practitioner's behalf.

The delegating nurse reviews the MOLST form and advance directives at admission, at each reassessment, after any hospitalization or readmission and when the resident's condition changes, and confirms the copy in the record is the most recent one (ADM-03, HCS-03).
The Manager tells the resident's practitioner and representative if the record shows a document that appears outdated or conflicts with the resident's current wishes, and records that notice.

A resident who has decision-making capacity may accept or refuse any treatment. When a resident declines treatment, the staff member notifies the delegating nurse, who documents the informed decision and informs the practitioner and representative (HCS-04).
When a resident cannot make decisions, staff contact the resident's representative or agent named in the record, and follow the person's authority as documented (RR-09).

In a medical emergency, staff call 911 and follow the emergency response procedure. Staff check the resident's MOLST for any orders on resuscitation and follow the MOLST as written, and the Manager is notified at once (HCS-04).

Whenever a resident is transferred to an acute care facility, the nurse or Manager prepares the emergency data sheet and attaches a copy of the advance directive, MOLST form, power of attorney and guardianship order, if any. The original MOLST goes with the resident if required by the practitioner's order, with a copy kept in the record.

When a resident returns from a hospital stay, the delegating nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission, reviews any new or changed MOLST or directives and updates the record and service plan (COMAR 10.07.14.29, ADM-04).

All staff learn the location of MOLST forms and advance directives, and what to do in an emergency, at orientation and annually (STF-03). Direct care staff are told when a resident has a MOLST that affects emergency response.
At discharge or transfer to another setting, the Manager gives the resident or representative copies of directives and the MOLST form and includes them with transfer papers (ADM-06).

The Manager audits a sample of resident records quarterly to confirm that directives, MOLST forms and the admission checklist entries are present and current, and reports the findings in the quality assurance review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every resident is asked about advance directives at admission, documents answers and makes sure the documents are in the record and travel with the resident.
Reviews MOLST forms and directives at each assessment and after a hospital stay, documents informed refusals and prepares or reviews the emergency data sheet.
Know where documents are kept, call 911 in emergencies and follow the MOLST, and do not give legal advice.
Provide current documents and tell staff about changes in wishes.

Copies of advance directives, mental health advance directives and MOLST form in the resident record

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and students of [AGENCY NAME], including the Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, delegating nurse, medication technicians and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of each resident's personal, financial and health information, to ensure records are released only as Maryland law permits, and to ensure [AGENCY NAME] meets the HIPAA privacy, security and breach requirements that apply to it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps confidential all resident case discussion, examination, treatment and records. Only persons directly involved in a resident's care may be present during case discussion, examination or treatment, unless the resident or the resident's representative permits otherwise. Resident records are released only with the written consent of the resident or representative, or as permitted by the Maryland Confidentiality of Medical Records Act (Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3). Records may also be released when the resident is transferred to another facility and when required by law. The Assisted Living Manager shares resident information with the Department of Health (OHCQ) as needed for its oversight. Records are disposed of only in the manner Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 allows. [AGENCY NAME] will determine whether it is a HIPAA covered entity. If it is, it will adopt and follow the HIPAA privacy, security and breach notification procedures below. Confidentiality protections apply whether or not HIPAA applies.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a resident, in any form (paper, electronic or oral), that relates to the resident's health, care or payment for care.

A health plan, health care clearinghouse, or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with a standard transaction covered by HIPAA, such as electronic Medicaid billing.
A person who is providing, supervising or coordinating the resident's care or services, or whom the resident or representative has permitted to be present.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its privacy or security, unless a low probability of compromise is shown through a documented risk assessment.
The person with legal authority to act for the resident, as documented under policy RR-09.

procedures: Upon hire, and before having access to resident information, each staff member signs a confidentiality statement and receives training on this policy. The Assisted Living Manager keeps the signed statement in the personnel record (STF-05).

Staff discuss a resident's condition, care or treatment only with persons directly involved in the resident's care, and only in a private place where others cannot overhear. Staff do not discuss residents in hallways, dining areas, or common areas, or on social media or personal devices.

Staff conduct examinations, treatments, personal care, and medication administration discreetly. They close doors or privacy curtains and limit those present to people directly involved in care, unless the resident or representative permits otherwise. Any permission is documented in the resident record.

Paper records are stored in a locked cabinet or room. Only staff who need the information to do their jobs may access them. Records are never left unattended in common areas. Electronic records require individual passwords and are never shared between users.

Before releasing any record to a person outside the facility, the staff member checks that the request is from the resident or representative with signed written consent, or that a legal basis applies (transfer to another facility, a requirement of law, or access allowed by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3). If unsure, the staff member refers the request to the Assisted Living Manager before releasing anything.

A consent to release is in writing, signed and dated by the resident or representative, and identifies the information to be released, the recipient and the purpose. The staff member files the consent in the resident record. The consent copy and a log entry record each release.

When a resident is transferred to a hospital or another facility, the nurse or manager sends the information necessary for continuity of care with the transfer documents (see HCS-04 and ADM-06). The transfer is noted in the record.

The Assisted Living Manager provides resident information to OHCQ surveyors and investigators on request, as needed for their oversight. Staff direct all surveyor requests to the manager or alternate manager.

Staff do not release resident information to law enforcement, attorneys, insurers or the media except as the law requires or with valid consent. The Assisted Living Manager reviews each such request and records what was disclosed, to whom and when.

The Assisted Living Manager decides in writing, within [30] days of licensure and again at least annually, whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity. The decision considers whether it conducts standard electronic transactions, such as Medicaid Community Options waiver billing. The decision, date and reasoning are kept in the compliance file.

If [AGENCY NAME] is a covered entity, the Assisted Living Manager designates a privacy official and a security official (see Responsibilities) and adopts written HIPAA privacy and security procedures, including sanctions for workforce members who violate them (45 CFR 164.530).

If a covered entity, [AGENCY NAME] provides each resident or representative a Notice of Privacy Practices at admission (45 CFR 164.520), asks the resident or representative to acknowledge receipt in writing, and posts the notice in the facility. Uses and disclosures of PHI follow 45 CFR 164.502.

If a covered entity, a resident or representative's written request to inspect or obtain a copy of the resident's records is handled under 45 CFR 164.524. The privacy official responds within the federal time limit (generally 30 days). Any denial is documented and the reason given in writing.

If a covered entity, the security official conducts and documents a security risk analysis and puts administrative, physical and technical safeguards in place (45 CFR 164.308). The risk analysis is reviewed at least annually and whenever systems change.

Any staff member who suspects an unauthorized access, use or disclosure of resident information reports it to the Assisted Living Manager immediately, and in all cases the same day. The manager investigates, takes steps to limit harm, and documents what happened.

If a covered entity, the privacy official performs a documented breach risk assessment. When a breach of unsecured PHI is confirmed, [AGENCY NAME] notifies each affected resident, or the representative, without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery (45 CFR 164.404). Notices to the federal government and the media are made where 45 CFR Part 164 requires.

Records are destroyed only after the retention period in REC-01 (5 years after discharge) has run, and only in the manner Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 permits. Paper records are shredded or incinerated, and electronic media are wiped or physically destroyed. A destruction log lists the resident, record and date, and the person who destroyed it.
The Assisted Living Manager reviews privacy complaints, incidents and audit results as part of the quality assurance plan (GOV-04) and retrains staff when problems are found.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, provides resources for secure record storage and systems, and receives the annual report on privacy compliance.
Enforces this policy, decides on record releases, makes and documents the HIPAA covered-entity determination, cooperates with OHCQ, and investigates suspected breaches.

responsibilities.role: Privacy Official and Security Official (if covered entity)
responsibilities.duty: Maintain the HIPAA privacy and security procedures, Notice of Privacy Practices, access requests, risk analysis, breach assessments and notifications. May be the manager or a designee.
Protects PHI in nursing assessments and communications, and ensures that information sent with transfers is limited to what is needed for care.
Sign the confidentiality statement, access only the information needed for their jobs, and report any suspected violation immediately.

documentation: Signed staff confidentiality statements and privacy training records
Signed resident or representative consents to release information
Log of records released outside the facility
Written HIPAA covered-entity determination and annual review
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments, access requests and responses (if covered entity)
Security risk analysis, breach risk assessments and breach notices (if covered entity)
Record destruction log

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], especially those involved in marketing, screening, admission, care planning, and discharge
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] admits and cares for residents without discrimination, treats every resident with dignity and individuality, and gives residents with limited English proficiency or disabilities meaningful access to information and services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admitting a person or in providing care because of race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, physical disability or mental disability. Each resident is treated with dignity and individuality, as the Resident Bill of Rights provides. Admission screening considers only the care-needs and safety criteria in COMAR 10.07.14.23B–C and the facility's licensed level of care, never a protected characteristic. [AGENCY NAME] provides free interpreter and translation services to residents and representatives with limited English proficiency, and reasonable accommodations to residents with disabilities.

definitions.definition: Race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, physical disability or mental disability.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part fully in the services offered.

A change to a policy, practice, communication method or physical setting that gives a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the services, unless it would fundamentally alter the program or create an undue burden or direct threat that cannot be reduced.

A person who is fluent in English and the resident's language, and who is trained to interpret accurately and impartially. A resident's family member or another resident is not used unless the resident specifically requests it and it is documented.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager ensures that marketing materials, the admission application, and the resident agreement state that [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of the protected characteristics above.

During pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the screener evaluates only the person's care needs, the Resident Assessment Tool results, and the safety criteria that COMAR 10.07.14.23B–C allow. The screener does not ask about or consider race, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity or disability as a reason to decline admission.

If a person is not admitted, the manager records the specific care-need or safety criterion relied upon and the date. The manager gives the reason to the applicant or representative. The record is retained for audit.
Before using any decision tool or screening question, the manager reviews it to make sure it does not screen out persons because of a protected characteristic.

At first contact and at admission, staff ask each resident and representative about their preferred language and any communication needs. The answer is recorded in the resident record and the service plan.

When a resident or representative has limited English proficiency, staff use a qualified interpreter or a telephone/video interpreter service at no cost to the resident. Staff use an interpreter for the pre-admission screening, resident agreement, Bill of Rights, consent forms, service plan meetings, grievances, and any significant change in condition or discharge discussion.

The Assisted Living Manager arranges translated or plain-language versions of key documents (Bill of Rights, resident agreement, grievance procedure, emergency instructions) in the languages most commonly needed by residents. When a translation is not available, a qualified interpreter reads the document aloud and staff note it in the record.

Staff do not require a resident to provide their own interpreter. Staff may use a family member or friend only at the resident's informed, documented request, and never for sensitive matters when the resident has not agreed.

For residents with hearing, vision, speech or cognitive disabilities, staff provide appropriate communication supports, such as large print, reading documents aloud, written notes, sign-language interpreters or assistive devices.

A resident or representative may request a reasonable accommodation orally or in writing. The Assisted Living Manager evaluates each request promptly, talks with the requester, and decides within [5] business days if practicable. The decision, the reason, and any alternative offered are documented.

Staff honor each resident's right to practice their religion, express their gender identity, and observe their cultural, dietary and personal-care preferences, within the limits of safety and other residents' rights. These preferences are recorded in the service plan.
Staff address residents by the name and pronouns the resident requests. Staff use respectful language and do not use slurs or demeaning remarks.

Any resident, representative, or staff member who believes discrimination or harassment has occurred may report it to the Assisted Living Manager. A grievance is handled under RR-02. Retaliation is prohibited. The manager investigates, takes corrective action, and documents the outcome.
The Assisted Living Manager trains all staff on nondiscrimination, cultural humility and language access at orientation and at least annually (STF-03), and records attendance.

The manager reviews admission and discharge decisions, accommodation requests, and discrimination complaints at least annually as part of the quality assurance plan (GOV-04), and corrects any pattern identified.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, funds interpreter and translation services, and ensures that no discriminatory admission or retention practices exist.
Oversees compliance, makes and documents admission and accommodation decisions, arranges language services, investigates complaints, and trains staff.
Applies only the care-needs and safety criteria at screening and documents the basis for any decision not to admit.
Treat all residents with dignity, use interpreters when needed, and report suspected discrimination.

documentation: Screening records showing the care-need or safety basis for any non-admission
Resident preferred-language and communication needs in the record
Interpreter use log (date, language, interpreter, topic)
Reasonable accommodation requests and decisions
Nondiscrimination training records
Discrimination-related grievances and outcomes

policies.title: Resident Representative
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, delegating nurse, admissions staff, and all staff who communicate with residents' families or legal decision makers
policies.purpose: To ensure that the identity and authority of each resident's representative are verified and documented, that representatives act only within their actual authority, and that representatives receive the notices and invitations that Maryland assisted living rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes a resident representative only when the person's authority is documented in the resident's record. The resident's own wishes and decision-making rights come first. A representative acts only within the authority granted by the legal instrument or by State law, and [AGENCY NAME] does not recognize a representative who goes beyond that authority. [AGENCY NAME] invites the representative to service plan meetings when the resident lacks capacity, and notifies the representative of incidents, any use of restraints, and any relocation or discharge. Before finalizing this policy, the Assisted Living Manager will confirm the list of persons who may be recognized as representatives against the current COMAR 10.07.14 representative provision and update this policy if needed.

definitions.definition: A person who is legally authorized under a written instrument or State law to make decisions or receive information for a resident, to the extent of that authority.
The document that grants authority, such as a power of attorney, health care agent designation under an advance directive, guardianship order, or other document recognized by Maryland law.
The resident's ability to understand information, appreciate the consequences, and communicate a decision. Capacity is decision-specific and may change over time.

procedures: At pre-admission and admission, the manager or nurse asks each resident whether they want someone to act for them or receive information on their behalf, and who. The resident's choice is noted in the record.

The manager asks for a copy of every authority instrument (power of attorney, health care agent designation, guardianship order, or other document) and checks the name, scope, effective date, and any limits. If the document or authority is unclear, the manager seeks clarification from the resident or the person's attorney before relying on it.

The manager records in the resident record the representative's name, relationship, address, phone number, the type and scope of authority, the date verified, and the staff member who verified it. A copy of the instrument is placed in the record.
Where a representative's authority is limited (for example, financial only, or health care decisions only when the resident lacks capacity), the record and the face sheet say so, and staff are told.

A person with no documented authority, such as a family member or friend, is not treated as a representative. Staff may share information with that person only with the resident's permission, and the permission is recorded (RR-07).

Staff do not accept direction from a representative that goes beyond the authority granted by the instrument or State law, including direction to withhold a resident's own rights, contact with others, or information the resident is entitled to. The manager reviews any such request, explains the limit to the representative, and documents the discussion.

A resident who has capacity keeps the right to make their own decisions, even when a representative is named. Staff talk with the resident first. A representative's authority takes effect for a decision only when the instrument or State law allows it.

When there is a question about the resident's capacity, the delegating nurse reports it to the resident's practitioner for evaluation and records the result. The manager does not decide that a resident lacks capacity.

The manager invites the representative, in writing or by phone, to each service plan meeting when the resident lacks capacity, and invites the resident always (ADM-04). The invitation, date and attendance are recorded.

Staff notify the representative of incidents involving the resident as required by SAF-02, of any use of a restraint as required by SAF-04, and of any relocation within the facility or discharge as required by ADM-02 and ADM-06. The notice is recorded with the date, time, method and person notified.
The representative is given the Resident Bill of Rights with the resident, and the signed acknowledgment is placed in the record (RR-01).
The representative's contact information is checked at each reassessment, at least every 6 months, and updated promptly when the representative or the resident tells staff of a change.

When a representative's conduct appears contrary to the resident's interests, or suggests abuse, neglect or exploitation, staff report it to the manager immediately and the manager follows SAF-01, including mandatory reporting. The manager also records the concern.

When authority ends (for example, revocation, guardianship change, or the resident regaining capacity), the manager gets documentation if available, updates the record, and tells affected staff the same day.
The manager reviews representative records at least annually for completeness as part of the quality assurance plan (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies and documents representative authority, ensures notices and invitations are sent, and resolves questions about the limits of authority.
Includes the representative in service plan meetings and change-of-condition notifications, and refers capacity questions to the practitioner.
Collect the authority documents and contact information at admission and enter them in the record.
Consult the record to confirm who may receive information or make decisions, and never assume authority.

documentation: Copy of each authority instrument
Representative information and scope-of-authority entry in the resident record
Resident's permission to share information with non-representatives
Service plan meeting invitations and attendance
Notifications to the representative (incidents, restraints, relocation, discharge)
Notes on any request denied because it exceeded the representative's authority

policies.title: Adult Medical Day Care, Voluntary Programs and Resident Work Duties
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, activities staff, direct care staff, and admissions staff
policies.purpose: To ensure that attendance at adult day care and any structured program is voluntary, that the availability and policies of adult medical day care are disclosed to residents in the resident agreement, and that residents perform work only by consent and with appropriate compensation.
policies.policy: Attendance at adult day care or any structured program is voluntary, and no resident is required to attend as a condition of admission or continued residence. If adult medical day care is available through or arranged by [AGENCY NAME], its availability and policies are disclosed in the resident agreement. A resident may perform work for the facility only with the resident's consent and with appropriate compensation, or with a documented decision to decline pay. The duties are described in the resident record, and the resident may stop at any time without retaliation. For residents on the Medicaid Community Options Waiver, these protections also support the choice and autonomy requirements of the federal home and community-based services settings rule (42 CFR 441.301(c)). Disclosure of adult medical day care policies in the resident agreement is a policy that the Office of Health Care Quality reviews at survey.

definitions.definition: A community-based program, separate from the assisted living residence, that provides health, therapeutic and social services during the day to adults who need them.
Any group, outing, class, day program or structured activity that a resident chooses whether to attend.
Any task done for the facility, such as helping in the kitchen, garden, laundry or office, that a staff member would otherwise perform or that benefits the facility rather than only the resident.
Payment for work at a rate that is lawful and fair for the work performed. It may be waived only when the resident has made an informed, documented decision to decline pay.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager states in the resident agreement whether adult medical day care is available, who provides it, the days and hours, any fee or charge, how transportation is handled, and the policies that apply (RR-04). If adult medical day care is not available, the agreement says so.

At admission, the manager or admissions staff reviews that section of the agreement with the resident and representative and explains in plain language that attending is the resident's choice. The resident or representative signs the agreement, and a copy is given to them.

Staff do not make admission, retention, room assignment, fee changes, or service levels depend on a resident's attendance at adult day care or any other program, unless the resident has freely chosen it in writing.

If a resident chooses adult medical day care, the manager coordinates with the day care provider. The coordination covers schedule, transportation, medications, communication about changes in condition, and the service plan (ADM-04). The resident's choice and the arrangements are documented.

For a resident on the Community Options Waiver, the manager confirms that the services billed to the waiver are consistent with Maryland Medicaid rules and the resident's plan of care, and that adult medical day care is not billed or arranged in a way that conflicts with the waiver rate (GOV-06).

A resident may decline or stop attending any program at any time. Staff respect the decision, do not pressure or punish the resident for declining, and record the choice. The delegating nurse and activities staff review whether the service plan should be changed.
Activities offered by [AGENCY NAME] are optional. Staff invite residents and offer alternatives and one-to-one options for residents who choose not to join (DL-02).
The facility does not require any resident to do work for the facility. A staff member who asks a resident to help with tasks must refer the request to the Assisted Living Manager first.

If a resident asks to do work, or is offered a work opportunity, the manager meets with the resident, and with the representative if the resident lacks capacity, to discuss the task, schedule, expected hours, compensation, safety, and the resident's right to stop at any time.
The manager confirms the resident is physically and mentally able to do the task safely, with input from the delegating nurse or practitioner if there is doubt.

The resident gives written consent to the work. The consent states the duties, hours, pay rate or a statement that the resident has chosen to decline pay, and that the resident may stop at any time without retaliation.

The manager sets compensation at a lawful rate that is fair for the task. Wages are paid and recorded in the resident's funds account when applicable (RR-05). The manager checks State and federal wage laws before approving any work arrangement.
The duties and the resident's consent are described in the resident record and the service plan. The duties are reviewed at least every 6 months at service plan review.

Residents cannot do work that is part of staff duties required by regulation, such as staffing, personal care of other residents, medication administration, or supervision, and cannot do work that is unsafe.

If a resident stops working, staff accept this without comment or retaliation and update the record. A resident's refusal or decision to stop does not affect services, room, relationships with staff, or the resident agreement.
The manager reviews all resident work arrangements and program participation records at least annually as part of the quality assurance plan (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves any resident work program, ensures it complies with wage and labor law, and ensures that programs remain voluntary.
Writes the resident agreement disclosure, approves work arrangements, arranges adult medical day care coordination, and prevents pressure or retaliation.
Evaluates safety for work duties and day care, and updates the service plan.

responsibilities.role: Activities staff and direct care staff
responsibilities.duty: Offer activities as choices, respect refusals, and refer any request for resident work to the manager.

documentation: Resident agreement section on adult medical day care availability and policies
Signed consent for each resident work duty, including compensation or documented decision to decline pay
Description of duties in the resident record and service plan
Payment records for resident work
Records of resident choices to attend, decline or stop programs
Coordination notes with the adult medical day care provider

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, delegating nurse, and admissions staff
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] admits only persons whose needs it can safely meet within its licensed level of care, that a Resident Assessment Tool is completed before admission, and that the facility meets the admission rules in COMAR 10.07.14.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only after a pre-admission screening and a Resident Assessment Tool completed within 30 days before admission. Admission is only within the facility's licensed level of care (Level 1, 2 or 3). [AGENCY NAME] does not admit a person who needs more than intermittent nursing care, treatment of a stage 3 or 4 skin ulcer, ventilator services, skilled monitoring with a fluctuating acute condition, or monitoring of an uncontrollable chronic condition. It does not admit a person who is dangerous to self or others when the danger cannot be eliminated, or who is at high risk for health or safety complications that cannot be managed. These limits do not apply when a licensed general hospice program delivers the services through its plan of care. Decisions are based on care needs and safety, never on a protected characteristic (RR-08).

definitions.definition: The State-required assessment form used to evaluate a person's health, functional and psychosocial needs before admission and at each reassessment (ADM-03).
Level 1 (low), Level 2 (moderate) and Level 3 (high). The license states the bed count and the level, and a resident may be served only within the licensed level.
Nursing care provided at intervals rather than continuously, as determined by the delegating nurse and consistent with COMAR 10.07.14.
The registered nurse who has a signed agreement with [AGENCY NAME], has completed the Board of Nursing-approved course, and assesses residents and delegates tasks (HCS-03).

procedures: Admissions staff takes each inquiry, explains the services, licensed level of care, and the admission limits, and records the date, the contact, and the person's general needs.

The manager checks that the licensed level of care and bed count cover the care the person is likely to need. If the person's needs exceed the licensed level, the manager does not proceed and tells the person why, and suggests other options.

The delegating nurse or other qualified person meets with the applicant, and the representative if there is one, and where possible visits the person where they now live. The screener reviews medical records, diagnoses, medication list, practitioner orders, functional status, cognition, behavior, and history of falls, wandering or aggression.

A Resident Assessment Tool is completed for the applicant within the 30 days before the planned admission date. If the admission is delayed past the 30 days, or if the person's condition changes, the RAT is redone before admission. The screener signs and dates it.
The screener obtains a practitioner's written information about the applicant's diagnoses and any medical orders, and confirms with the practitioner or the nurse any condition that raises a concern.

The delegating nurse checks the applicant against each admission exclusion: more than intermittent nursing care; stage 3 or 4 skin ulcer treatment; ventilator services; skilled monitoring with a fluctuating acute condition; and monitoring of an uncontrollable chronic condition. If any applies, the person is not admitted, unless the hospice exception is met.

The manager and nurse evaluate whether the applicant is dangerous to self or others, or at high risk for health or safety complications that [AGENCY NAME] cannot manage, considering history, current behavior, and available staffing and supports. They consider whether reasonable steps, such as a changed service plan or added supports, can eliminate or control the risk. The reasoning is documented.

If the applicant is enrolled with a licensed general hospice program, the manager obtains the hospice plan of care and confirms in writing which services the hospice will deliver, so that the exclusions are managed by the hospice (HCS-08). The manager documents that the hospice exception applies.

The manager checks that staffing, including the delegating nurse's schedule and medication technician coverage, is sufficient to meet the applicant's needs without lowering care for current residents (STF-01).

If the applicant has dementia or related needs, the manager confirms whether the applicant's care can be provided under the facility's license, and whether an Alzheimer's special care unit disclosure and placement under HCS-05 is needed.

The manager makes the admission decision with the nurse and records it, with the date and the basis, using only care-needs and safety criteria. If the applicant is declined, the manager gives the applicant or representative the reason in writing and a list of alternatives where possible (RR-08).

Before or on admission, the manager reviews the resident agreement, fees, and Bill of Rights with the resident and representative, and obtains signatures (RR-01, RR-04). The manager confirms the representative's authority (RR-09).
On admission, the nurse reviews the resident's medications and orders, and arranges for a medication regimen review within 14 calendar days of admission (HCS-01, HCS-03).

The service plan is completed within 30 calendar days of admission, based on the RAT and the nursing assessment (ADM-04). Until then, staff follow the interim care instructions from the screening and practitioner orders.

The manager places the screening, RAT, practitioner information, hospice documents, admission decision and agreement in the resident record (REC-01) and reports any admission data to the State as REC-02 requires.
The manager reviews admission decisions and any admissions made outside these criteria at least quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Sets the licensed level of care and ensures that staffing and resources match the residents admitted.
Makes the final admission decision, ensures the 30-day RAT requirement is met, and ensures no one is admitted outside the licensed level or admission criteria.
Completes or oversees the pre-admission screening and RAT, evaluates the admission exclusions, and arranges the 14-day medication regimen review.
Handle inquiries, gather documents and arrange agreement signing.

documentation: Inquiry and screening notes
Resident Assessment Tool completed within 30 days before admission
Practitioner information and orders
Written admission decision with the basis, or the reason for declining
Hospice plan of care and exception documentation, if applicable
Signed resident agreement and Bill of Rights acknowledgment
Evidence of the 14-day medication regimen review and 30-day service plan

policies.title: Bed and Room Assignment and Change in Accommodation
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, delegating nurse, admissions staff and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To ensure that residents are assigned rooms in a way that meets Maryland space and occupancy rules, and that a resident is not moved within the facility except under the resident agreement, with proper notice and the resident's consent.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns beds and rooms in compliance with COMAR 10.07.14: no more than 2 residents per room, with at least 80 square feet in a single room and 120 square feet in a double room. A resident is not relocated within the facility except as the resident agreement provides. A nonemergency relocation requires at least 5 calendar days' notice and the resident's consent, and is documented in the record. Residents are told before a roommate change and their input is considered where possible. Bed and room assignment and change in accommodation are policies that the Office of Health Care Quality reviews at survey.

definitions.definition: Any move of a resident to a different room or bed within [AGENCY NAME], including a move to another unit.
A relocation that is not needed to protect the immediate health or safety of the resident or others.
A relocation needed immediately to protect the health or safety of the resident or others.
Any change in the person who shares the resident's room, including a new roommate or a move of the current roommate.

procedures: The manager keeps a current room inventory listing each room, its measured square footage, its capacity (no more than 2 residents), and the bathrooms serving it. The manager checks the inventory against the licensed bed count and the space standards at least annually and after any physical change.

No single room is assigned for use by more than one resident, no double room is assigned to more than 2 residents, and no room is used if it falls below 80 square feet (single) or 120 square feet (double).

The manager checks that common space, toilets, sinks, and tubs or showers remain sufficient for the number of residents (35 square feet of common space per bed; 1 toilet and sink per 4 residents; 1 tub or shower per 8 residents). If a new bed would put the facility under any standard, it is not filled.

At admission, the manager assigns a room based on the resident's care needs from the Resident Assessment Tool, safety, mobility, the resident's preferences, and compatibility with any roommate, and records the assignment. The resident agreement tells the resident the circumstances in which a relocation may happen.

Before a roommate is assigned, staff tell the current resident about the proposed roommate change and ask the resident's views. The manager takes input into account where possible and records the discussion, including any objection and how it was resolved.
Before a new resident moves in with a roommate, the manager tells the new resident about the room arrangement and the roommate and records the resident's response.
Residents who cannot get along with a roommate may ask to move. The manager reviews the request promptly, tries to resolve the issue, and offers a move if a suitable room is available.
A resident is relocated within the facility only in accordance with the resident agreement. A resident's relocation is never used as a penalty or retaliation, including for a complaint or grievance.

For a nonemergency relocation, the manager discusses the reason with the resident, and with the representative if there is one, and explains the proposed new room. The manager gives written notice at least 5 calendar days before the move.

The written notice states the reason, the proposed new room, and the date. The resident or representative consents in writing. If the resident or representative does not consent, the move does not take place, and the manager explores other options. If the issue involves changed care needs that the facility cannot meet, the manager follows ADM-05 and ADM-06.
The manager documents the notice date, the reason, the resident's consent, the new room, and the date of the move in the resident record. The manager tells the representative of the move (RR-09).

For an emergency relocation, staff move the resident only as far and as long as needed to protect health or safety. The manager tells the resident and the representative as soon as possible and documents what happened, why, when and who was told. The manager follows the 5-day notice and consent process if the resident is to stay in the new room long term.

The delegating nurse reviews whether a move affects the service plan, such as falls risk, supervision, proximity to staff or the dining room, or a change of level of care, and updates the plan (ADM-04). If a significant change has occurred, the nurse completes a full assessment within 48 hours.
Staff help the resident to move belongings safely, including inventory of personal property and replacement in the new room, and make sure the resident is oriented to the new room (RR-05).

If a requested move would require a different level of care than licensed, or the facility cannot meet the resident's needs, the manager follows ADM-05 and ADM-06 (discharge or transfer with 30 calendar days' notice for nonemergency discharge).
The manager reviews room assignments, moves, notices, and consents quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that licensed capacity and space standards are met and that building changes are reviewed against COMAR 10.07.14.
Makes bed and room assignments, gives notice and obtains consent for relocations, handles roommate changes, and keeps the room inventory.
Evaluates care needs for room assignment and updates the service plan or assessment after moves.
Help residents move safely, protect personal property, and report roommate concerns to the manager.

documentation: Room inventory with square footage and capacity
Resident room assignment record
Roommate change discussions and resident input
Written 5-calendar-day relocation notice and signed consent
Emergency relocation notes and notifications
Service plan updates after a move
Notice to the representative

policies.title: Resident Assessment Tool and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, Alternate Manager, direct care staff and all residents (Level 1, 2 and 3)
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident's needs are assessed before admission and reassessed on schedule and after changes in condition, so that the service plan and staffing match what the resident actually needs and the resident can be served safely within the licensed level.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes the Resident Assessment Tool and a nursing assessment for each resident before admission (COMAR 10.07.14.22 and .28B(1)). The delegating nurse reassesses each resident fully within 48 hours after a significant change of condition or a nonroutine hospitalization, as nursing practice and the resident's condition require, and at least annually (.28B(2)). The assessment is reviewed at least every 6 months (.22; .28B(4)). Each assessment documents whether awake overnight staff is needed (.28B(5)). The delegating nurse reassesses a resident within 48 hours of readmission after a hospitalization, after a stay of 15 or more days in a skilled nursing facility, or after a significant change (.29B). A resident who self-administers medications is reassessed by the delegating nurse every quarter (.31D(2)).

definitions.definition: The standardized assessment instrument required by the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) that scores the resident's functional, cognitive, behavioral, medication and communication needs and is used to set the level of care and build the service plan.
The registered nurse under a signed agreement with [AGENCY NAME] who performs nursing assessments, delegates nursing tasks and monitors residents as required by COMAR 10.07.14 and COMAR 10.27.11.

As used by [AGENCY NAME]: a change in a resident's physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status that is not expected to be brief and that affects the resident's care needs, safety or ability to be served at the current level of care.
A hospital admission or emergency stay that is not a planned or scheduled procedure with an expected return to baseline.

procedures: Before admission, the Assisted Living Manager (or designee) schedules the delegating nurse to complete the Resident Assessment Tool and a nursing assessment. The RAT must be completed within 30 days before the date of admission. An RAT completed earlier than 30 days before admission is repeated.

The delegating nurse completes the assessment by direct observation and interview of the resident, and reviews the practitioner's information and the medication list. The nurse also consults the resident's representative, family and other providers, with the resident's permission.
The delegating nurse signs and dates the RAT and nursing assessment. The Manager files both in the resident record on or before the day of admission.
The Manager uses the results to confirm that the resident can be served at the program's licensed level and does not have a condition the program cannot serve (see ADM-01 and ADM-05).

The delegating nurse completes the full reassessment within 48 hours after a significant change of condition or a nonroutine hospitalization, as nursing practice and the resident's condition require. Direct care staff report the change to the Manager and delegating nurse the same day it is noticed (see HCS-04).

If the delegating nurse decides a full assessment is not needed within 48 hours, the nurse writes the reasons in the resident record on the day of the decision. The full assessment is then completed within 7 calendar days of the change or hospitalization.

The delegating nurse reassesses a resident within 48 hours of readmission after a hospitalization, after a stay of 15 or more days in a skilled nursing facility, or after a significant change. The nurse documents the reassessment and any changes to orders, medications and the service plan.

The delegating nurse completes a full reassessment at least once every 12 months. The Manager keeps a tracking log with each resident's admission date, last full assessment date and next due date, and checks the log at least monthly.
The delegating nurse reviews each resident's assessment at least every 6 months, and the review is dated and signed. The review is held together with the 6-month service plan review (see ADM-04).

If the review shows a score change in cognition or behavior, self-administration of medications or communication, the delegating nurse notifies the resident's practitioner for evaluation. The delegating nurse also updates the service plan and records the notification and the plan changes.

At every assessment, the delegating nurse documents whether awake overnight staff is needed for this resident. The Manager reviews the result against the staffing plan and adjusts overnight staffing when needed (see STF-01).

For each resident who self-administers medications, the delegating nurse reassesses the resident's ability to do so every quarter and documents the result. If the resident can no longer self-administer safely, the nurse changes the medication plan and informs the Manager (see HCS-02).
The Manager shares assessment results with the resident and, with the resident's permission, the representative. The Manager invites them to the service plan meeting (see ADM-04).
If an assessment shows that the resident's needs exceed the licensed level or fall within a condition the program cannot serve, the Manager begins the process in ADM-05 the same day.

The Manager files all assessments, reviews, reassessment notes and the reasons for any delayed full assessment in the resident record (see REC-01), and reports overdue assessments to the Quality Assurance committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Completes the nursing assessment, RAT, reassessments, 6-month reviews and quarterly self-administration reassessments; decides and documents any delay in a full assessment; notifies practitioners of score changes.
Schedules assessments, keeps the tracking log, adjusts staffing based on the awake overnight determination, and ensures all assessments are filed and on time.
Observe and report changes in condition to the Manager and delegating nurse the same day.
Reviews timeliness of assessments at least quarterly.

documentation: Resident Assessment Tool with date and signature of the delegating nurse
Nursing assessment and every reassessment note
Written reasons for any full assessment not completed within 48 hours, and the completion date within 7 calendar days
6-month review documentation and practitioner notifications for score changes
Awake overnight staffing determination at each assessment
Readmission reassessment within 48 hours
Quarterly self-administration reassessment
Assessment tracking log

policies.title: Service Plan
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, direct care staff, residents and resident representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a written, individualized service plan, developed with the resident, that says what services the resident receives, when and how often, how, and by whom, and that is kept current as needs and preferences change.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a written service plan for each resident within 30 calendar days of admission (COMAR 10.07.14.28D). The plan is based on the Resident Assessment Tool and nursing assessment, and states the services to be provided, when and how often, how, and by whom. The plan is reviewed at least every 6 months and sooner when the resident's condition or preferences change significantly. The resident, and at the resident's request a representative or family member, is invited to every service plan meeting (.28A). The plan addresses the resident's special care needs (.28C). For residents who receive Community Options Waiver services, the plan is person-centered and coordinated with the waiver plan of service, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: The resident's written plan describing the services [AGENCY NAME] will provide, including when, how often, how and by whom.
Needs related to falls, pressure ulcer risk, diabetes, oxygen, enteral feeding, Foley catheter, ostomy, therapeutic medication levels, mental illness and disruptive behaviors.
A person the resident has chosen, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident (see RR-09).

procedures: Within 3 business days of admission, the Manager schedules the service plan meeting. The meeting date must fall within 30 calendar days of admission. The Manager accommodates the schedules of participants where possible.

The Manager invites the resident to every service plan meeting. If the resident asks, the Manager also invites the representative or a family member. The Manager documents the invitation and who attended.
Before the meeting, the delegating nurse prepares a draft from the Resident Assessment Tool, nursing assessment, practitioner orders and the resident's stated preferences (see ADM-03).
